title: What Do We Mean When We Say 'F*ck AI'?: Moral Panic, Semantic Indeterminacy, and the Reification of Techno-Capitalism
abstract: Academic and (increasingly) public resistance to artificial intelligence (AI) often blurs the line between legitimate critique of techno-capitalist exploitation and (inflated) existential risk. Moreover, discourse around AI can sometimes resemble a "moral panic" where an apparently clear and identifiable scapegoat is targeted in lieu of the complex systemic problems that are causing (genuine and justified) social anxieties. However, AI is not a monolith. In this paper, we explore the environmental, political, and socio-technical consequences of the semantic indeterminacy of discourse about "AI" in conjunction with the increasing moral panic encompassing these technologies. We argue that since the umbrella term "AI" lacks a coherent, singular referent, the moral panic about AI inadvertently reifies the concept of an autonomous, singular agent with inherent and often autonomous tendencies, which aligns with corporate narratives. Hence, well-intentioned critique, activist pushback, and public protest paradoxically amplifies hype-based discussions of AI, thus validating the "threat" narrative that tech leaders deploy to exaggerate their products' capabilities and market value, further consolidating and centralising their political and socio-economic power. Moreover, if "AI" does not refer to a unified class of technologies, then policy intended to govern "AI" will systematically (and necessarily) fail. title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy as a New Form of Academic Literacy
abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is profoundly transforming the epistemological foundations of higher education. Universities are no longer faced solely with the challenge of integrating new technologies into teaching and learning processes; they are increasingly called upon to rethink the very nature of knowledge production, assessment, academic integrity and professional skills. This article argues that AI literacy should be understood as a new form of academic literacy, which goes beyond technical competence to encompass critical, ethical, epistemological and pedagogical dimensions. Drawing on recent international studies and emerging frameworks for AI literacy, the article discusses the implications of AI literacy for curriculum design, staff development and institutional transformation in higher education.

title: Developing and Validating an AI-Literacy-Integrated Teaching Acceptance and Readiness Scale for Mathematics Teachers
abstract: The global shift toward cultivating students’ AI literacy requires teachers to reconceptualize curricula and pedagogical practices. However, research has focused primarily on teachers’ use of AI tools, overlooking their readiness to integrate AI literacy as a learning goal, particularly in mathematics education. In response, this study developed and validated the AI-Literacy-Integrated Teaching Acceptance and Readiness Scale for Mathematics Teachers (AILTAR-M). The instrument was theoretically organized around two domains: (1) Acceptance , comprising four constructs adapted from the Technology Acceptance Model (Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Attitude toward Use, and Behavioral Intention); and (2) Readiness , encompassing Perceived AI Literacy as a self-reported cognitive dimension and Teaching Self-Efficacy as a motivational dimension. Psychometric evaluation with 549 mathematics teachers in China supported a 29-item, six-factor structure. Exploratory factor analysis ( n = 174) yielded a six-factor solution explaining 69.7% of the variance, and confirmatory factor analysis ( n = 375) demonstrated acceptable model fit (CFI = .938, TLI = .931, RMSEA = .063, SRMR = .038). The instrument exhibited strong internal consistency (α = .899– .943) alongside satisfactory convergent and discriminant validity. title: Refining collaborative AI literacy: A systematic review of human–AI collaboration competency and AI literacy measures
abstract: With the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and its growing role in solving complex problems, human–AI interaction has evolved into a new dimension, where AI is increasingly perceived as a collaborative partner. However, current AI literacy frameworks focus on technical knowledge and ethical use, often neglecting the ability to collaborate effectively with AI as a standalone construct. Conceptualized under the umbrella of AI literacy, the boundaries of human–AI collaboration competency need to be refined in order to create common ground for advancing research and measurement of this essential ability. This systematic review synthesizes 17 studies conducted in higher education settings to examine how human–AI collaboration competency is represented and measured within existing AI literacy scales. The findings reveal that human–AI collaboration is rarely explicitly assessed, let alone as a distinct construct. Some studies included a small number of items that could implicitly refer to collaboration competency or context, but most included no such representation. Drawing on these findings, we propose theoretical implications regarding contexts and factors that should be considered when developing new items, and measurement implications for three possible sub-factors of human–AI collaboration competency: coordination, communication, and metacognition. title: From AI Literacy to AI Fluency
abstract: As frontier artificial intelligence transitions from generative assistance to autonomous agentic systems, the rapid automation of entry-level knowledge work is hollowing out traditional corporate training grounds, transforming organizational structures from pyramids into "diamonds." In response, higher education's prevailing focus on basic AI literacy—teaching students how to operate software tools—is proving insufficient. This article argues that the modern landscape demands AI fluency: the advanced cognitive judgment required to establish operational boundaries, allocate human oversight based on the consequence of errors, and adversarially audit synthetic outputs. Because automated workplaces no longer provide the entry-level apprenticeships where professional judgment historically formed, higher education must structurally redesign its pedagogy. This requires shifting from tool-centric instruction to a two-stage model of consequence-based learning: embedding deliberate cognitive friction within classroom coursework, followed by scalable, high-stakes experiential learning (such as clinical-model internships and client-facing projects) before graduation. Ultimately, this shifts institutional assessment away from the final polished artifact and toward a student's capacity to evaluate, reconcile, and assume responsibility for AI-driven outcomes.

title: Assessing AI Literacy in High-School and University Students – A Robust Performance-Based Test Using Authentic Scenarios
abstract: We present the development of a performance-based AI literacy assessment instrument designed for high-school and early-stage university students. The influence of AI in society, research, and education is continously growing making AI literacy more and more important. As existing AI literacy assessments largely rely on self-assessment or are vulnerable to rapid technological developments in AI, the need for a robust, objective tool arises. The test combines a competency-based framework, informed by the work of the OECD and European Commission, with Multiple True-False questions embedded in authentic, scenario-based vignettes reflecting everyday AI applications. Its design focuses on three dimensions: input into AI systems, output of AI systems, and ethics and sustainability, while relying on fundamental AI concepts to ensure long-term relevance. Currently undergoing piloting and psychometric validation using Rasch modelling, the instrument is available in English and German and aims to help educators identify students’ learning needs and foster their AI-related competencies.

title: Institutionalizing AI Literacy in Teacher Preparation
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping teaching, learning, assessment, and professional judgment across P–16 education. This chapter presents a competency-based microcredential framework designed to prepare teacher candidates for responsible AI use before clinical practice. The framework positions AI literacy as a professional competency grounded in instructional design, ethical stewardship, data privacy, equitable access, human–AI collaboration, and reflective judgment. It moves from foundational understanding to applied classroom implementation through modules focused on responsible AI adoption, AI fluency, prompt literacy, AI limitations and risks, instructional design in AI-rich environments, classroom guardrails, and a culminating AI Integrity Statement. Drawing on literature synthesis, stakeholder feedback, policy analysis, and professional standards, including TPACK and UDL-informed approaches, the chapter offers an adaptable framework for guiding responsible implementation across educator preparation contexts.

title: Teaching AI Literacy for Public Health Practice
abstract: This study evaluated an AI-driven assignment in an undergraduate public health course to enhance AI literacy among students preparing for health-related careers. Amid growing AI use in academia—and uncertain ethical perceptions—the project addressed the need for responsible AI application in public health and healthcare management education. Designed with constructivist strategies (experiential, inquiry-based, project-based, and collaborative learning), the assignment tasked student groups with creating AI-scaffolded community health promotion plans. Implemented in online sections, the project leveraged tools such as ChatGPT and ClaudeAI for data analysis, decision-making, and communication material development. Pre- and post-curriculum assessments, using the Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAILS) , showed significant gains in overall AI literacy, particularly in confidence, and evaluation skills, though ethical understanding improved minimally. Qualitative feedback highlighted students’ surprise and appreciation for using AI professionally. If expanded to all sections, the project will impact more than 200 students per year across three majors. The intervention underscores AI’s potential role in disease surveillance, health communication, and equity-focused interventions, aligning with CEPH and CAHME competencies (Appendix 1). title: A systematic review examining conceptualizations and implementation pathways alongside empirical evidence of artificial intelligence literacy in higher education from 2021 to 2025
abstract: Through a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of peer-reviewed publications (2021–2025), this study mapped the conceptualization, implementation pathways, and empirical evidence of AI literacy in higher education, drawing on a screened corpus of 56 peer-reviewed publications. Three research questions guided this review: (1) how AI literacy is conceptualized in higher education; (2) what effective pathways have been implemented for developing AI literacy among students and educators; and (3) what empirical evidence reveals about AI literacy levels, dimensions, and interdimensional relationships among students and educators. Findings reveal that conceptual fragmentation persists in definitions, frameworks, and dimensions (RQ1), with cognitive and behavioral dimensions more frequently emphasized than affective and ethical dimensions. This pattern is reflected in implementation pathways (RQ2), where many initiatives emphasize operational proficiency, tool use, and prompting, while critical reflection, ethical engagement, and longer-term developmental outcomes receive less consistent attention. Empirically (RQ3), student-focused studies commonly report moderate overall AI literacy, whereas educator-focused studies indicate readiness concerns in several higher-order, pedagogical, and ethical domains; because measures, samples, and contexts differ across studies, these findings should not be interpreted as a direct statistical comparison between populations. Mean vectors differed by participation type(Pillai = .098, F(8, 872) = 5.64, p < .001). This descriptive pattern does not establish that the patterns of participation-type differences vary across the four variables. title: BIBLIOTECAS ACADÉMICAS NA ERA DA INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL GENERATIVA: análise crítica dos desafios e oportunidades para os profissionais da informação
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is profoundly transforming how information is produced, accessed, and used within academic contexts, presenting both challenges and opportunities for libraries and information professionals. This research critically examines the implications of integrating GenAI into academic libraries, focusing on ethical, social, and professional challenges, as well as opportunities for service innovation and skills development. Using a qualitative methodology based on a narrative literature review, the study identifies institutional guidelines, emerging applications of GenAI in library services, and essential competencies for information professionals. The findings highlight the central role of AI literacy, continuous professional development, and the adoption of ethical and responsible principles. The study concludes that, despite the challenges identified, GenAI offers significant potential to strengthen academic libraries as key spaces for learning, innovation, and equitable access to knowledge.

title: TEACHER PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT FOR AI LITERACY IN UPPER SECONDARY EDUCATION: A COMPARATIVE SYNTHESIS OF COMPETENCY AREAS.
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become widely available in educational settings, raising questions that extend beyond operational use. This study aims to compare recurrent AI literacy competency areas across a deliberately delimited corpus and to analyze the considerations they suggest for teacher professional development in upper secondary education. This qualitative, bibliographic-documentary study is based on a deliberately delimited corpus of ten publications assembled for a focused conceptual discussion rather than through a reproducible search protocol. The corpus combines foundational definitions of AI literacy, international competency frameworks, a recent K-12 review, a cross-sectional study involving 525 senior high school students in the Philippines, a review of teachers’ professional development needs for AI integration, a mixed-methods study on self-directed professional development with ChatGPT, and a qualitative study with 20 elementary and middle school teachers in Delhi. The sources were organized around four literature-informed comparative areas: conceptual understanding and awareness of AI systems; pedagogical use of generative AI as a resource for teaching and learning; critical evaluation of AI outputs, including uncertainty and bias; and ethics, authorship, data protection, and human-centered responsibility, understood as both a dedicated and cross-cutting area. title: Librarians and Teaching AI Literacy: A SWOT Analysis
abstract: This Open Educational Resource (OER), developed within the Erasmus+ GEDIS project (Gender Diversity in Information Science: Challenges in Higher Education), presents the findings of a participatory SWOT analysis examining librarians’ capacity to teach artificial intelligence literacy (AI literacy). The study was conducted using the Nominal Group Technique (NGT), involving 90 librarians from school, public, academic and special libraries. The analysis highlights strengths and opportunities, including existing information literacy competencies, teaching skills, openness to acquiring new knowledge and growing user interest. At the same time, it identifies weaknesses and threats, such as insufficient knowledge of artificial intelligence, limited resources, rapid technological developments and inadequate recognition of librarians’ roles. The findings indicate that librarians already possess relevant competencies for teaching AI literacy, although their levels of preparedness vary. They emphasise the need for targeted support, continuous professional development and the strengthening of professional competencies. The resource is intended for librarians, educators, students and other interested users. It can be used in higher education, professional development and activities related to information literacy and AI literacy.

abstract: This article examines the role of self-education in sustaining continuous professional development among academic staff at Ukrainian technical universities amid the combined pressures of digital transformation and wartime disruption. It focuses on how lecturers adapt their professional learning practices to air-raid alerts, power outages, unstable internet connectivity and unequal access to digital infrastructure. Drawing on relevant academic literature and reported professional experiences, the study identifies several interconnected vectors of self-directed learning, including artificial intelligence (AI) tools, informal collegial exchange, open educational resources, asynchronous webinars, independent academic reading and low-technology reflective activities. Particular attention is devoted to AI-assisted learning and its potential to facilitate lesson planning, academic writing, information synthesis and pedagogical innovation. Simultaneously, the article highlights significant challenges associated with inaccurate AI-generated content, excessive technological dependence and the potential deterioration of critical reading, analytical reasoning and independent scholarly judgement. Furthermore, it considers how disparities in electricity supply, internet connectivity and technological resources may exacerbate existing inequalities in professional development opportunities. title: Toward calibrated AI readiness in K–12 school-based practice: the roles of AI-related epistemic vigilance capacity and governance clarity
abstract: The responsible use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in K–12 schools requires professionals to evaluate AI-generated information while maintaining ethical boundaries and accountability for decisions. This two-phase study examined calibrated AI readiness, defined as self-reported readiness to verify AI outputs, recognize ethical boundaries, and retain responsibility for AI-assisted professional decisions. In Phase 1, 425 school-based professionals completed a survey assessing AI-related epistemic vigilance capacity, autonomous regulatory motivation, governance clarity, and calibrated AI readiness. Structural equation modeling indicated that epistemic vigilance capacity ( β = .675, p < .001) and governance clarity ( β = .270, p < .001) were positively associated with calibrated AI readiness, whereas autonomous regulatory motivation was not a significant predictor ( β = .076, p = .156). An exploratory observed-score analysis found no significant interaction between epistemic vigilance capacity and autonomous regulatory motivation. In Phase 2, 25 school psychologists and school counselors participated in a one-month online pilot training program delivered through Moodle and Zoom. Self-reported calibrated AI readiness, measured using the same nine items as in Phase 1, increased descriptively from a pre-training mean of 4.20 to a post-training mean of 4.84 on a five-point scale. title: AI-Driven Workforce Reskilling and Organizational Performance of Insurance Companies in South-South Nigeria
abstract: This study examined the relationship between AI-driven workforce reskilling and organisational performance among insurance companies in South-South Nigeria. A cross-sectional survey research design was adopted, with primary data collected through structured questionnaires. The study population comprised 20 selected insurance companies in South-South Nigeria, and a census sampling technique was employed. The respondents consisted of managers from the selected companies. AI-driven workforce reskilling served as the predictor variable, while organisational performance was measured using operational efficiency, service quality, and innovation performance. The instrument's validity was established through academic supervisors' assessments, while reliability was confirmed using Cronbach's alpha coefficients exceeding 0.70. The hypotheses were tested using Spearman's rank-order correlation at a 0.05 significance level. The findings revealed significant relationships between AI-driven workforce reskilling and all three dimensions of organisational performance. The study concluded that AI-driven workforce reskilling significantly predicts organisational performance among insurance companies in South South Nigeria. The study recommended that insurance companies establish continuous AI reskilling programmes to equip employees with practical competencies in AI-enabled systems, data analytics, automation, and digital process management. abstract: This study examines the Influence of Artificial Intelligence on students' Critical thinking and Problem-solving Skill in Business and Entrepreneurship Education in Kwara State, Nigeria. Two purposes were raised from which two research questions and two hypotheses were generated. A quantitative explanatory study strategy was employed, utilizing primary data gathered via structured questionnaires distributed to 150 students from three universities in the state. The sample was intentionally chosen to encompass essential factors, such as the frequency of AI tool utilization, degrees of AI adoption, and students’ self-assessed problem-solving and critical thinking skills. Data analysis utilized both descriptive and inferential statistical techniques. The regression models indicate a moderate positive association between Artificial Intelligence and critical thinking skills, and a moderate positive correlation between Artificial Intelligence and problem-solving abilities. The findings indicate that although Artificial Intelligence markedly improves students' critical thinking and problem-solving abilities, there is an urgent necessity for organized Artificial Intelligence training initiatives and faculty development. title: Guide to implementing artificial intelligence projects in the public sector
abstract: This practical guide aims to assist public institutions with the design, development and responsible implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) projects, from identifying the problem to deploying the solution in real-world settings. It proposes a clear three-phase road map (exploration, development and real-world implementation), structured into specific steps, with trigger questions, key decisions and minimum deliverables at each stage. The approach combines public value, technical data and governance, which helps determine when to use AI, how to compare it to non-AI-based alternatives and how to manage the risks associated with data, bias, privacy, security and accountability. The guide includes practical tools —such as checklists, institutional readiness criteria, prototyping, testing and continuous monitoring— that are in line with the principles of AI accountability. It is aimed at management and at technical, legal and operational teams, and it seeks to establish a common language that facilitates useful, auditable and sustainable AI projects in the public sector.

title: Artificial Intelligence Ethics and Responsible Technology Adoption in Organizations
abstract: Even as organizations are turning to artificial intelligence to find ways to work more efficiently not keeping pace with the changes in the governance that will be necessary to do so responsibly. This paper explores the connection between AI ethics governance practices and responsible technology adoption, based on an analytical sample of 120 organizations from financial services, healthcare, technology, and the public sector. Eight of these governance practices were rated for depth of implementation and were aggregated to create a governance maturity index, which was then correlated with a composite responsible adoption index, commitment to leadership, and ethics Awareness among employees. Results indicate that practices related to data protection and risk assessment are most embedded (3.83 and 3.48 on a scale of 1–5 for extent of embedding, respectively), while transparency, fairness auditing, and stakeholder engagement are only partially embedded (2.88, 2.78, and 2.51, respectively). Governance maturity is highly correlated with responsible adoption (r = 0.72), and leadership commitment and employee awareness are important in the relationship beyond the relationship with maturity (R² = 0.62). The results suggest that there is a practice-to-outcome gap, which is greatest in smaller companies and in the public sector, and the paper ends with recommendations for future priorities and research directions.

title: SLR: Board-level AI Governance in Financial Services
abstract: This project pre-registers the protocol (v1.4) for a systematic literature review on board-level governance and oversight of AI and algorithmic risk in financial services. The review asks: what is known about board-level governance and oversight of AI-related risks in financial services, and what gaps remain in the banking sector in developing economies? Searches will run on Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection (2017 to date, English), with PRISMA 2020 screening, eligibility criteria, quality appraisal, second-reviewer reliability checks, citation chasing, and open data sharing. Included studies will be tagged by sector, governance level, and regulatory frameworks referenced. Expected outcomes: a documented, reproducible corpus; a descriptive map of the field; and a gap analysis feeding the literature chapter and framework design of a linked PhD study on AI governance in Nigerian banking. The review replicates and extends a documented exploratory proposal-stage retrieval of 88 records (2021-2026), which is not carried forward into the review corpus. This registration updates v1.3 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/4VAPN); no searches were executed under v1.3.

title: FROM BOARDROOM ILLITERACY TO ALGORITHMIC ACCOUNTABILITY: WHY AI LITERACY IS NOW A FIDUCIARY DUTY FOR EVERY BOARD
abstract: This study examined the emergence of AI literacy as a fiduciary duty for company directors in Nigeria and globally. The background was that boards which were previously judged on financial literacy now governed algorithms that decided credit scoring, recruitment, asset integrity and pricing, yet Diligent Institute (2026) found that only 18% of directors were confident to discuss AI risks. The research adopted a doctrinal legal methodology, using content analysis of primary statutes and codes including CAMA 2020 Section 305, UK Corporate Governance Code 2024 Principle J and Provision 23, EU AI Act 2024 Article 99, NDPA 2023 Section 24, and secondary materials including FTC v Rite Aid (2025), Caremark and Marchand v Barnhill_ on duty of oversight, and ISO/IEC 42001:2023. The findings were that AI risks were not IT risks but core governance risks, exposing boards to regulatory fines up to €35m or 7% turnover under EU AI Act, liability under NDPA 2023, reputational damage from algorithmic bias, and operational leakage from generative AI hallucination and model drift. The study found that lack of AI literacy constituted breach of duty of care, skill and diligence under S.305 CAMA 2020 because directors who did not understand model cards, training data and bias testing could not effectively challenge management. abstract: In the years following the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, more than half of U.S. states have published formal guidelines around AI usage in K-12 education, creating a record of largely independent state education departments responding to a shared technological disruption. In this work, we analyze publicly available AI usage guidance documents from 35 states in the U.S. and Puerto Rico. We compare the guidance in these documents across various dimensions, including pedagogy and instruction, audience, actionability, workforce and career readiness, responsible use and equity, and alignment with state-level demographics and administrative capacity. Finally, we investigate who authored these documents and their cited sources, identifying epistemic foundations underlying their claims. We find that guidance priorities converge on topics anchored in laws such as data privacy and academic integrity, each addressed in 97% of documents. While most documents mention equity of access (86%) and algorithmic bias (97%), fewer discuss specific marginalized populations. Across documents, there is a common framing of urgency around AI integration to prepare students for workforce readiness (86%) and promote loosely-defined personalized learning (86%), which is not matched by specific guidance for capacity-building, actionability, or accountability. title: Information Literacy Readiness in North Indian University Libraries: A Historical Comparative Analysis of 2012 Survey Evidence
abstract: Purpose: This paper re-examines historical evidence on information-literacy readiness in five selected state and five selected central university libraries in North India, focusing on ICT infrastructure and organisational preparedness. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study uses descriptive secondary analysis of a doctoral thesis’s comparative and state-library survey chapters. Only figures traceable to source tables or explicit table-based statements are retained. No new survey, imputation, or inferential testing was undertaken. Findings: The comparative table reports 303 computers across five state university libraries and 205 across five central university libraries. Internet access was recorded in four of the five selected state libraries, while the comparative narrative reports access in all five central libraries. These historical figures do not establish per-user availability, service reliability, or learning outcomes. Other percentages were excluded pending source-table verification. Originality/Value: The paper presents historical findings as a baseline rather than a representation of current conditions. It proposes a conceptual framework covering ICT access, digital-resource management, information and AI literacy, staff capabilities, ethical governance, and assessment. title: Student Agency in AI-Assisted English Language Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education has created new opportunities for personalized learning, adaptive instruction, and learner autonomy. However, concerns remain regarding students' ability to maintain independent decision-making, critical engagement, and ownership of their learning processes when interacting with AI technologies. This study aims to systematically review the development of student agency in AI-assisted English language learning, focusing on agentic practices, critical AI literacy, AI-supported scaffolding, and psychological and pedagogical influences. Employing a qualitative systematic literature review (SLR) approach, six publications published between 2025 and 2026 were examined using qualitative content analysis and cross-study thematic synthesis. The findings reveal four interconnected themes. First, student agency develops dynamically through receptive, participatory, and co-creative practices, reflecting increasing independence and control over AI-mediated learning activities. Second, critical AI literacy strengthens students' ability to evaluate AI-generated information, recognize technological limitations, and make informed learning decisions. Third, AI-supported scaffolding facilitates English language development, particularly listening and writing, through personalized materials, adaptive feedback, and interactive learning opportunities. title: UNIVERSITY LECTURERS' ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CURRICULUM INTEGRATION INTENTIONS: THEORY OF PLANNED BEHAVIOR EVIDENCE FROM ASIA
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming business practices and increasing the need for higher education institutions to integrate AI-related competencies into business curricula. However, empirical evidence on the behavioral factors influencing university lecturers’ intentions to integrate AI, particularly in Asian higher education, remains limited. Grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), this study examines the determinants of lecturers’ intentions to integrate AI into business curricula. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 235 university lecturers from several Asian countries, and the data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The model examines the effects of attitude, subjective norms, and self-efficacy while incorporating AI-related education and prior AI use as background factors. The findings show that self-efficacy is the strongest predictor of AI integration intention, followed by attitude, whereas subjective norms have no significant effect. AI-related education indirectly strengthens intention through attitude and self-efficacy, while prior AI use primarily enhances perceived capability. This study suggests that competency development and AI-focused faculty training may be more important than normative pressure in promoting AI curriculum integration among lecturers in the sampled higher education contexts.

title: From General AI Ethics to Child-Sensitive Governance: Evidence from National AI Strategies
abstract: As artificial intelligence systems increasingly permeate the institutional environments shaping childhood and adolescence, the governance architecture underpinning these technologies demands rigorous empirical scrutiny. This study examines how UNICEF’s nine child-sensitive AI principles become visible across sovereign national AI strategy documents (N=27N=27N=27) through complementary rule-based lexical detection and contextual semantic retrieval measures. The empirical findings reveal a significant structural divergence: while explicit lexical matches remain concentrated in a minority of strategies (26.92%), with a predominant focus on long-term human-capital preparedness (P08), semantic proximity highlights moderate thematic attention in developmental well-being (P01) and a pronounced nadir in fairness and non-discrimination (P03). Non-parametric tests confirm no significant association between lexical density and semantic similarity (ρ=0.1379,p=0.5019\rho=0.1379, p=0.5019ρ=0.1379,p=0.5019). To address these gaps, the study advances a reproducible dual-track computational screening framework and operationalizes developmental ethics concepts—such as transitional paternalism, relational autonomy, and the mitigation of overtrust and manipulative design—providing an upstream diagnostic instrument for embedding proportionate Child-Rights AI Impact Assessments (CR-AIAs) within iterative public policy evaluation cycles.

title: AI-generated content-plagiarism versus institutional silence: comparative insights on responses of higher education to rapid technological changes in China and Japan
abstract: This study seeks to elucidate how the higher education systems of China and Japan have addressed the issue of plagiarism exacerbated by generative artificial intelligence (AIGC-plagiarism) and the insights gained from these responses. As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated with higher education, the age-old problem of plagiarism has resurfaced with greater intensity and elusiveness, sweeping across universities worldwide. Although no definitive consensus exists regarding the precise definition of AIGC-plagiarism, this conceptual ambiguity does not preclude its broad recognition as prohibited academic conduct. The relationship between cutting-edge technologies and higher education appears to have reached an impasse, yet the majority of Chinese institutions have maintained a stance of silence, while the Chinese government has shown concern but refrained from taking formal action. This research comparatively examines the response strategies to AIGC-plagiarism by the Japanese government and 359 universities, which share similar systemic and institutional contexts with their Chinese counterparts, and reaches a conclusion that the practice of “No Copy + Exceptions” emerges as a particularly instructive approach. title: Harmonizing the Principles of the EU AI Act with Indonesian AUPB for Transparent Algorithmic Governance
abstract: Background: The digitalization of government procurement through Indonesia’s E-Catalog system has shifted certain functions traditionally performed by human bureaucrats to algorithmic systems that exercise what may be termed “algorithmic discretion” in product ranking and recommendation. Legal challenges arise because Indonesia’s administrative law framework, particularly Law No. 30 of 2014 on Government Administration, remains largely anthropocentric and inadequately addresses algorithmic systems acting as “invisible bureaucrats.” This creates an accountability gap when algorithmic decisions produce hidden biases that adversely affect providers’ rights. title: From centralised artificial intelligence to democratic systems: African Union-aligned pathways for economic justice and the right to development
abstract: Four decades after the adoption of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development (DRtD), artificial intelligence (AI) is being deployed across Africa’s financial services, digital identity systems, public administration and cross-border trade. Prevailing models of AI governance, however, are highly centralised concentrating data ownership, algorithmic control and economic value in a small number of predominantly external actors. This chapter pursues three objectives. First, it examines how centralised AI governance undermines the right to development (RtD) by weakening democratic accountability, limiting public participation and reinforcing structural inequality. Second, it establishes the RtD, as recognised in the DRtD and article 22 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, as the normative foundation for AI governance in Africa, and clarifies the chapter’s conception of economic justice. Third, it develops an African Union (AU)-aligned framework for democratic AI governance. Drawing on doctrinal analysis of African and international instruments, including Agenda 2063, the AU Digital Transformation Strategy, the AU Continental AI Strategy and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Protocol on Digital Trade, the chapter finds that existing approaches prioritises efficiency and innovation over participation, accountability and distributive justice. title: Decolonising the algorithmic state: The right to development as a pan-African framework for artificial intelligence-driven governance in Zimbabwe
abstract: This chapter contends that the emergence and proliferation of the algorithmic state in Zimbabwe has the potential to replicate systems of coloniality and recreate colonial patterns that manifest in the following dimensions: discrimination, extraction and exclusion. This underscores the need for a purposive and deliberate recalibration of the algorithmic state through the lens of the right to development (RtD). In response to criticism that the RtD is hazy, vague, ambiguous, unenforceable and state-centric, this chapter provides a concrete definition and explanation of decolonisation in algorithmic governance, which is the reallocation of algorithmic power from external suppliers or vendors and colonial data frameworks to inclusive accountable, participatory and redistributive systems rooted in indigenous legal pluralism. Utilising the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development (1986) (DRtD) which commemorates its 40th anniversary in 2026 in tandem with the African Charter on Human and Peoples Rights (article 22) as well as emerging African scholarship on algorithmic governance, the chapter proposes a pan-African rights-based approach, model and framework for the decolonisation of the algorithmic state. title: Governing artificial intelligence in public services: accountability, transparency and democratic AI governance
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how democratic governments can regulate artificial intelligence (AI) in public services through accountable, transparent and institutionally governable frameworks. It addresses the governance gap between rapid AI adoption and limited democratic regulatory oversight by proposing the Transparent-Accountable-Governable (TAG) Framework. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a qualitative conceptual research design using comparative policy analysis. It critically synthesises interdisciplinary literature in public administration, digital governance and AI ethics alongside the OECD AI Principles (2025), UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021), the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework (2023) and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (2024) to develop the TAG Framework. Findings The analysis argues that trustworthy AI depends upon the interaction of transparency, accountability and governability rather than ethical principles alone. The proposed TAG Framework provides an institutional governance model applicable across welfare administration, healthcare, taxation, policing and disaster management. Research limitations/implications This is a conceptual study and therefore does not empirically validate the TAG Framework. title: Custody-First AI Governance: A Reference Architecture for Canadian Public Bodies
abstract: This paper specifies an open-source reference architecture for governing AI systems in Canadian public bodies, and fixes the protocol for validating it at Technology Readiness Level 4. The architecture answers a gap that current governance tooling leaves open: no product carries a clock that runs for as long as the consequences of a decision last. On their publicly documented capabilities, existing tools record that an assessment happened. They do not keep the assessment reviewable after the model, the reference data and the supplier have changed. The design is custody-first. Every registered AI system carries a decision class, a consequence horizon, an evidence horizon computed over named dependencies, and an accountable office. The Canadian federal rulebook (Directive on Automated Decision-Making, Algorithmic Impact Assessment, Policy on Service and Digital) is built in as versioned controls, not loaded as a plug-in, together with the AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service and the guiding principles for responsible AI. Every finding is a record in its own right: requirement, evidence slice, result, confidence, authority, timestamp. It is retained for the consequence horizon of the system it assesses. Reviewers can validate, reject, modify or annotate any finding, and an append-only log preserves the sequence of every decision. Erasure leaves a tombstone, never a silent gap. title: AI and Feminist Worldmaking in Technofascist Times
abstract: Drawing on her forthcoming book, 10 Ways to Stop Technofascism (MIT Press, 2027), D'Ignazio will contextualize the rise of ''technofascism'' – the collusion of large technology firms with authoritarian, extractive, and anti-democratic political agendas. While we can see technofascism manifesting globally, it is not inevitable and we do not have to accept a future predicated on accumulation, violence, and exclusion. To that end, D'Ignazio will highlight the importance of feminist worldmaking through technology. Drawing from the large-scale participatory AI project described in Counting Feminicide (MIT Press, 2024), she will describe how the research team built technology with data activists and journalists to enact alternative epistemological approaches to information science that center care, memory and justice. These and other experiments in ''solidarity technology'' (Souza De Alvear et al. 2026) place knowledge and information in the service of informatic futures that foster life, living, and vitality.

title: Peer workers as bridge-makers: symbolic representation and co-production of services for stigmatized groups
abstract: Public services often struggle to reach stigmatized populations, as professionals may lack the trust, cultural knowledge, or standing needed to engage them effectively. Peer workers—people involved in service delivery who share an identity or lived experience with the population served—are increasingly used to bridge this gap. This study investigates these bridge-making benefits of peer workers through the lens of symbolic representation and co-production. Specifically, we analyze which approaches of “symbolic peer co-production” enable peer workers to engage effectively with both professionals and stigmatized groups, and the variety of roles played by peer workers with different identities as bridge-makers. Using a case study of HIV prevention in São Paulo, we conducted a documentary and social media analysis to examine how symbolic representation and lived experience help peer workers to act as bridge-makers between professionals and stigmatized groups. The findings suggest that peer workers enhance service accessibility by leveraging shared identities and experiences, reducing stigma, and building trusting relationships. This study contributes a novel theoretical framework integrating symbolic representation and co-production, and offers insights for designing more inclusive public services for stigmatized populations.

title: A theoretical model of co-production of public goods and services: A Systematic literature review and thematic synthesis
abstract: This study examines the transformative role of co-production in delivering public goods and services across diverse public-service contexts. It aims to examine the nature, application, drivers, barriers, and reported outcomes of co-production. A systematic literature review with thematic synthesis was conducted using 10 peer-reviewed studies selected through predetermined eligibility criteria. The findings identified stakeholder engagement, knowledge integration, resource availability, and motivational drivers as recurring factors associated with effective co-production. The reviewed evidence indicates that co-production can facilitate citizen participation, knowledge exchange, service improvement, learning, and responsiveness to public needs. However, implementation can be constrained by unequal participation, power imbalances, limited financial and institutional resources, technological barriers, weak trust, and difficulties in consistently measuring outcomes. Based on the synthesis, the study develops the Integrated Co-Production Impact (ICI) Theory, which proposes that motivational drivers promote stakeholder engagement, engagement facilitates knowledge integration, and resource availability enables integrated knowledge to contribute to co-production effectiveness. title: Inclusive climate adaptation through intersectional co-production: gender- and disability-disaggregated evidence from southern Africa
abstract: Inclusive climate adaptation is widely promoted but remains under-evidenced in practice. This article examines an intersectional co-production process in urban and peri-urban southern Africa aimed at improving weather and climate information services, with particular attention to women and persons with disabilities. The study combines surveys, focus groups and interviews in Kanyama, Zambia, and Boane, Mozambique. The process included inclusive engagement and tailored communication materials to improve the usability of weather information. As a result of this process, community observers reported enhanced confidence, empowerment and perceived social status. Although the process led to outcomes of improved trust in, access to, attention to, and action on weather information across all groups, the gains were uneven. Women faced greater barriers to acting on information, while accessibility remained the main barrier for persons with disabilities. The article shows that intersectional co-production can advance representational and procedural justice and improve distributional outcomes. However, inclusion in process alone is insufficient to overcome structural inequality. It argues for climate services design and evaluation through an explicitly intersectional lens, with greater attention to disability inclusion, differentiated barriers, and justice-oriented measures of success embedded from the outset.

title: Balancing principles, power, and pragmatism: reflections on co-production in establishing national research priorities for women’s sport and physical activity
abstract: Interest in co-production within sport, exercise, and health sciences has grown in recent years. The use of this approach, however, is not without challenges. In this article, we share reflections on a co-produced project that sought to establish research priorities for women in physical activity, sport, and exercise on the island of Ireland. More specifically, we analyzed reflections from 17 public contributors-known as the Research Collective-and an interdisciplinary research team of 10 academics who collaborated to develop a survey, distributed nationally, to establish the research priorities. Our reflections highlighted persistent tensions between our ability to deliver our intended co-production approach while operating within structural constraints, including limited funding, institutional bureaucracy, and a short funding timeframe. We also identified challenges with relationship building and diversity, such as sustaining engagement beyond the project timeframe and ensuring representation of marginalized sub-groups. For the research team, these tensions and the need to compromise our approach carried an emotional weight that both shaped and was shaped by the (re)negotiation of power with the Research Collective. To support the advancement of co-production practice, we conclude by offering recommendations for researchers based on our learnings from this project.
authors: Emma S. Cowley, Denise Martin, Jennifer Murphy, Aoife Lane
